questions.article: Where the Muslim Brotherhood Went Wrong
questions.q: The editorial quotes the Prophet: “As you are, so will be the government upon you.” What does it conclude from this saying?
options: Government grows out of society, so minds must be prepared first; a system cannot be imposed
Yes. This was, in the author’s view, the Brotherhood’s mistake.
Power should be taken first and society reformed later
Not quite. The article says: Government grows out of society, so minds must be prepared first; a system cannot be imposed.
A ruler should be obeyed whatever he does
Not quite. The article says: Government grows out of society, so minds must be prepared first; a system cannot be imposed.
Good people always get good rulers at once
Not quite. The article says: Government grows out of society, so minds must be prepared first; a system cannot be imposed.
questions.rationale: “The government always emerges from society. It cannot be imposed from outside… If your society is not ready to accept your system, you have to wait and engage yourself in the task of preparing the minds of people.”

questions.article: Where the Muslim Brotherhood Went Wrong
questions.q: Sir Arthur Keith wrote that the Egyptians “were conquered not by the sword, but by the Koran.” Why does the editorial recall this?
options: To argue that the Quran is a political manifesto
Not quite. The article says: To show that peaceful sharing of the message achieves what force cannot.
To praise the early armies of Islam
Not quite. The article says: To show that peaceful sharing of the message achieves what force cannot.
To show that Egypt was never ruled by Muslims
Not quite. The article says: To show that peaceful sharing of the message achieves what force cannot.
To show that peaceful sharing of the message achieves what force cannot
Well done. “The power of the Quran is greater than the power of the gun.”
questions.rationale: The editorial offers the formula “dawah activism and political status-quoism,” and says the Quran is “a book of ideology,” not a political manifesto.

questions.q: A returning astronaut wanted to kiss the earth. How does the article contrast this with the response of a true believer?
options: The believer looks past the gift to the Giver and offers his deepest feelings to the Creator
Exactly. He “rises above creation and discovers his Creator.”
The believer avoids travel beyond the earth
Not quite. The article says: The believer looks past the gift to the Giver and offers his deepest feelings to the Creator.
The believer feels nothing for the earth
Not quite. The article says: The believer looks past the gift to the Giver and offers his deepest feelings to the Creator.
The believer prefers heaven to the earth
Not quite. The article says: The believer looks past the gift to the Giver and offers his deepest feelings to the Creator.
questions.rationale: “The one who does not believe thinks that the beauty of created things is actually intrinsic to these things… a true believer sees the beauty of the Creator in the beauty of creation.”

questions.article: Ritual Must Arise from the Spirit
questions.q: A man prayed in the mosque with every outward form correct, yet the Prophet sent him to pray again. Why?
options: He had missed a part of the ablution
Not quite. The article says: His prayer was mechanical and lacked the spirit of modesty.
He had prayed too quickly for others to follow
Not quite. The article says: His prayer was mechanical and lacked the spirit of modesty.
His prayer was mechanical and lacked the spirit of modesty
Right. Form without spirit is not worship.
He had prayed at the wrong time
Not quite. The article says: His prayer was mechanical and lacked the spirit of modesty.
questions.rationale: “However punctilious the worship in form, without the true spirit the performance of the ritual is invalid.”

questions.article: Ritual Must Arise from the Spirit
questions.q: During the first Haj, pilgrims worried that they had performed rites in the wrong order. The Prophet said, “There is no harm.” Where did he say real harm lies?
options: In performing Haj more than once
Not quite. The article says: In dishonouring a person.
In dishonouring a person
Yes. Where the spirit is present, a slip in form is tolerable.
In missing a day of the pilgrimage
Not quite. The article says: In dishonouring a person.
In asking too many questions
Not quite. The article says: In dishonouring a person.
questions.rationale: “There is no harm. There is no harm. Real harm lies in the dishonouring of a person.”

questions.q: By what process, according to the article, can a conditioned mind be de-conditioned?
options: Honest introspection – accepting others’ criticism and being one’s own strictest critic
Correct. The article calls these external and “self-hammering.”
Reading as widely as possible
Not quite. The article says: Honest introspection – accepting others’ criticism and being one’s own strictest critic.
Avoiding people who disagree
Not quite. The article says: Honest introspection – accepting others’ criticism and being one’s own strictest critic.
Moving to a new country
Not quite. The article says: Honest introspection – accepting others’ criticism and being one’s own strictest critic.
questions.rationale: “De-conditioning of the mind can only be done by one process alone, and that is introspection… Either one accepts the ‘hammering’ of others or one becomes one’s own worst critic.”

questions.q: Prophet Abraham advised his son to “change the threshold” after meeting one wife and to “maintain” it after meeting another. What made the difference?
options: The first was a stranger; the second was a relative
Not quite. The article says: The first complained of her hardships; the second was grateful in the same conditions.
The first was idle; the second worked hard
Not quite. The article says: The first complained of her hardships; the second was grateful in the same conditions.
The first complained of her hardships; the second was grateful in the same conditions
Yes. A great mission needs people free of complaint.
The first was poor; the second was wealthy
Not quite. The article says: The first complained of her hardships; the second was grateful in the same conditions.
questions.rationale: “For the great mission… the people who are suitable are only those who have the highest level of positive thinking, and who are free from all complaints.”

questions.q: Most people believe in life after death. Why, says the article, does this belief so rarely affect how they live?
options: They doubt that deeds are recorded
Not quite. The article says: Each group has added a self-made belief that its own salvation is assured.
Each group has added a self-made belief that its own salvation is assured
Well read. The article finds this among Muslims as much as others.
They have never been taught about it
Not quite. The article says: Each group has added a self-made belief that its own salvation is assured.
They think the Hereafter is very far away
Not quite. The article says: Each group has added a self-made belief that its own salvation is assured.
questions.rationale: “When other self-made beliefs are added to this belief, then believing in the life after life is almost as good as not believing in it at all.”

questions.q: How does the article advise us to look on failure?
options: As a sign to give up the goal
Not quite. The article says: As experience that can make us wiser and open a new path.
As a punishment to be endured
Not quite. The article says: As experience that can make us wiser and open a new path.
As experience that can make us wiser and open a new path
Right. When one opportunity ends, another appears.
As proof that plans are useless
Not quite. The article says: As experience that can make us wiser and open a new path.
questions.rationale: “When faced with failure, one must consider it as an experience and then move on to a new path… Failure can open even bigger doors of success for you.”

questions.q: In what sense does the article call old age “a prior notice”?
options: It tells a person to stop working
Not quite. The article says: It is a reminder that death and accountability before God are near.
It warns the young to respect their elders
Not quite. The article says: It is a reminder that death and accountability before God are near.
It is a reminder that death and accountability before God are near
Yes. The most unfortunate is one who draws no lesson from it.
It announces the end of one’s duties
Not quite. The article says: It is a reminder that death and accountability before God are near.
questions.rationale: “Old age is a prior notice of one’s death… Old age can shake up a person and make him conscious of the Hereafter.”
